question: How should someone with OCD deal with intrusive thoughts of disbelief and constant doubts about wudu?
asked: Brother Ahmad from London suffers from OCD and constantly gets bad thoughts that make him feel he might have left Islam, so he keeps renewing his Islam by saying the shahadah; he's frustrated and tired. Sister Faiza, also from England, has OCD about cleanliness: she always doubts her wudu, and after using the restroom she feels the floor is unclean and that she might have touched something on her way out, so she worries about the validity of her salah.
answer:
Now of course, the main feature of these questions is obsessive compulsive disorder, OCD. And for those of you that are unaware, to summarize, OCD is intrusive thoughts, usually relentless, that most of us would view as not normal. They're not something that we would consider to be rational; they seem to be just too irrational from our perspective. Again, from the perspective of those who are getting these thoughts, they think it is completely normal. So these are thoughts that keep on coming into one's mind, that drive the people who get them to be very anxious. And they are very specific thoughts; usually they're repetitive thoughts.

So for example, in both of these scenarios, if you looked at it: the first brother is saying that he's getting thoughts about ideas that make him think that he's not a Muslim anymore, and he's constantly renewing his shahadah over and over again throughout the day. And in the second part, the sister is worried about the tahara issues, the najasa issues, when she uses the restroom. When she does wudu, she puts her foot on the floor, and then she's worried that the floor might have najis on it. So she's acting in a manner that, again, would be termed OCD, obsessive compulsive disorder.

And this leads the people that are having these thoughts to do repetitive actions in an effort to neutralize, or in an effort to reduce, or in an effort to combat those anxious thoughts or those feelings or those sensations. And unfortunately, sometimes OCD even leads to a type of depression, sometimes even serious depression, and sometimes worse than this. So this is it in a nutshell. And again, this isn't a medical analysis; I'm simply saying, from our lay perspective, how those of us who don't have OCD view OCD.

And to respond to this, there are two angles, two ways to respond. The first of them is from an Islamic legal and theological standpoint, and that's what I'm going to talk a little bit about. The second is not my area of expertise, but I'll just talk generically, and that is from a psychological or a therapy perspective. I am not a psychiatrist. I am not trained in psychology. So it's not my area to advise you on specifics, but I will simply give you generic advice that is found in mainstream textbooks and whatnot of this nature, and also advise you to find a therapist. So these are two areas to respond to this OCD: firstly, from the fiqh and the theological side, and then secondly, some generic psychological or psychiatric advice that can help, inshaAllah, in this regard.

As for the Islamic perspective, as for the religious perspective, realize, dear brother and dear sister, realize, anyone who is having these types of thoughts, that Allah has not made the religion that difficult. Allah has not made the religion difficult. Allah says, "Allah wants ease for you." Allah wants ease, and Allah says, "There is no difficulty in this religion."

And one of the main principles of Islamic law: there is a section of Islamic law called the maxims of fiqh, al-qawa'id al-fiqhiyyah, and there are five primary maxims, and one of them is: that which is certain is not going to be gotten rid of by that which is doubtful. That which is certain is not going to be eliminated by something that is doubtful. And I need you to memorize this rule and then to apply it to all of these scenarios to the best of your capability.

So for example, that which is certain: you have wiped your hand; that is now certain. Then you lift your hand up, then a doubt comes: did I miss a small area over there? That is a doubt. The certainty: you have wiped your entire hand up until the elbow. That is certain. You have seen this, you have felt it. The certainty is that the floor is clean. That is certain. The default is that the floor in a Muslim household is going to be clean. You're talking about your own house; we're not talking about a public restroom, which, again, we're going to get to in a while, even that. But in your own house, the certainty, the default, is that everything should be clean. You should not be assuming that anything you touch or whatnot is najis. On the contrary, the default, or the certainty, is cleanliness. Then the doubt is what? Is there najis or not? So what is the principle of fiqh? That which is certain is not going to be eliminated because of something that is doubtful. So the certainty is what we will base our verdict on.

And of course this is based on many hadiths. Because you see, OCD is not a rare phenomenon. OCD exists in every society; it has existed since the beginning of time. And it is very likely that the companions who asked the Prophet ﷺ the following few questions we're going to mention also suffered from this type of very normal issue, and that is this OCD.

So for example, a person is saying, "O Messenger of Allah, I'm basically always thinking that I'm breaking my wudu, I'm passing gas. I'm always breaking my wudu, and I'm not sure. It's just a thought in my mind. I feel a sense, or I think I feel, but I'm not sure." What did our Prophet ﷺ say? Do not break your salah based upon those assumptions. Again, going back to this principle: al-yaqeen, the certainty, is not eliminated because of the doubt. What is certain? You are praying and you've done wudu. What is doubtful? Did something come out or not? Did I break wind? Was air released or not? This is doubtful. So what did the Prophet ﷺ say? Until you are certain. And how did he, in that particular hadith, raise the bar of certainty? He said, until you hear, or until the smell comes to you, so that you are now certain. And our scholars mentioned the purpose of these two is not that only these two count; the purpose is to achieve the level of certainty.

So if a person is certain that he has broken his wudu, if a person is certain that the arm has not been fully washed (so you go to the middle of the hand and then you stop in wudu), or if you know for a fact that there's najis on your hand or on your foot, in this case, okay, that's a separate story. Otherwise, the default is that you ignore that which is doubtful.

And in fact, in another hadith, we also get a companion that seems to be having an OCD that is about waswasa, or thoughts, just like our first brother, the same question that he asked. A man came to the Prophet ﷺ and he said, "O Messenger of Allah, I get thoughts in my head that are so evil that I would rather be," in one version, "torn apart before I utter those things from my tongue. I'm getting these bad thoughts all the time." And again, perhaps back then there weren't psychiatrists to analyze and to psychodiagnose; we don't know. But perhaps this was a companion that was also suffering from a type of OCD.

So he is saying, "O Messenger of Allah, I'm constantly getting these doubts that are very evil thoughts, very evil thoughts, and I would rather be torn to shreds than to verbalize them." Did the Prophet ﷺ tell him, "You have committed kufr every single time the thought comes"? Did the Prophet ﷺ tell him, "You have to do the shahadah multiple times a day"? On the contrary, the Prophet ﷺ calmed him down and said: your reaction is the essence of faith. Your reaction is the essence of faith.

What does this mean? Our scholars say: the fact that the man felt a type of anger or disgust at those thoughts, he didn't want to act upon them, he wants to get rid of them; the fact that the man is saying, "I would rather be torn apart before I verbalize these thoughts"; the fact that he says this, our Prophet ﷺ said that emotion of hating those bad thoughts is the essence of iman. SubhanAllah.

Therefore, dear brother in Islam, you do not have to verbalize the shahadah over and over again. Sure, you want to do dhikr and say la ilaha illallah, go for it, no problem. You want to do dhikr and say alhamdulillah, subhanAllah, no problem; do it a hundred times a day, excellent. But to think that you have become a kafir because of a thought that comes into your head? Not at all. You do not become, a'udhu billah, a kafir simply because of a waswasa, a doubt that is most likely coming from shaytan. Most likely it's not even coming from you. It's not even from you; it's from Iblis, it's from the shayatin. They're just whispering things into your ear.

And therefore, do not act upon these things. Feel a sense of "I wish it wasn't happening," and then that's it. You do not have to repeat the kalimah as if you have left Islam. As I said, we are separating between doing the kalimah as a statement of dhikr, which is fine, you may do it at any time, versus thinking that you have left the fold of Islam and then constantly returning back, quote unquote, because the questioner says, "I'm constantly re-accepting Islam." No, you have never left Islam such that you need to re-accept it. You are, alhamdulillah, a Muslim throughout all of these thoughts that are happening. So we do not open the door to these whisperings, to these waswasa, and we do not act upon them.

So my advice to all of our brothers and sisters that are suffering from this phenomenon known as OCD is that we should try our best to minimize, and we should realize that, alhamdulillah, the shari'ah does not make the religion difficult. We are not required, every single time we wipe our hand, to think, "Oh, is every single molecule, is every single spot done?" No. The default: you wipe it and you go to your elbow, and then that is it. If you even do it once, it is the minimum, and three times is of course the sunnah to do. Once you have done it, even once, that is it. The yaqeen is there, the certainty is there; you have done it. The same goes for your bathroom floor or any place that is in your house. The default is that it is not najis.

Now, in a public bathroom, by the way, if somebody were to say, "Okay, how about the public bathroom? I'm not sure what is in there." Guess what? Our Prophet ﷺ explicitly said that if you are going to the restroom, then anything that is on the floor there, once you walk a few steps, it is forgiven. It is forgiven. The hadith says that if a person steps in najis (because in those days there was no flushing toilet; there was excrement and waste everywhere, and it was common for a person to step in something like this), the Prophet ﷺ said, "The steps after it purify that which was on it."

So in other words, if you're wearing shoes and you walk into the public restroom, you just simply continue walking outward, and as you walk outward, what is at the bottom of the soles of your shoes is going to be forgiven. This is forgiven anyway. Therefore, do not make this such a big deal. The shari'ah is an easy shari'ah; the shari'ah is not requiring you to go to this level.

Therefore, from an Islamic perspective, dear brother and dear sister, and all of you who are listening that have symptoms that are OCD, understand that this is the simple principle: once you have done something that you should do, which is al-yaqeen, then you ignore all of the shakk that comes after it. You do not have to act upon it, and it does not affect the yaqeen.

Now, as for the psychological side of things, obviously I'm not an expert, so I strongly urge you to seek professional help in this regard. And there's some generic advice that is mentioned in the standard books that discuss this issue. Of them is that some psychiatrists say that your goal should not be that you need to eliminate the thought, because that is perhaps an unrealistic goal. Rather, the goal is to conquer it such that you are not acting upon it. So the goal is not that you're not thinking the thoughts. No, rather the goal is to conquer, so that even if the thoughts come, you are not going to be acting. Your goal is to control the action; it is not to control the thought. So that's one of the psychological tactics.

Also, some psychiatrists have advised: go ahead and agree even with the thought, but then realize you don't have to act upon it. Therefore, in this example, suppose that shaytan comes with the OCD, waswasa comes, and you think to yourself, "Oh, my hand did go all the way, but perhaps there's a molecule somewhere on my arm that the water didn't touch." In your mind, say, "You know what, maybe there is that molecule. Okay, but Allah does not require me to wash at the molecular level, so then I can ignore it." So then even embrace the thought, if it is going to allow you to not act on the action. Because the goal is that you don't make your life difficult. The goal is that Allah subhanahu wa ta'ala is not going to call you to task for something that is so trivial. You wiped your hand, and if some portion is left even after you wiped, you are forgiven. At the molecular level, Allah is not asking you to do that. And the same goes for all of the other aspects as well.

Also, some of the psychiatrists have mentioned: try your best to take care of your physical and mental health outside of the OCD issues, because anything that is going to affect your health will also trigger the OCD. Anything that's going to affect your mental state as well might make the OCD worse. So take care of your body, eat healthy foods, monitor your caffeine (how does caffeine affect you?), have good sleep habits, and make sure that you try to minimize stress in other areas. Because we don't want other stress to come; if that happens, it's going to cause your OCD to go into, if you like, extra drive mode, and we don't need to make it worse. Also, try to find friends that are going to help you, and stick around family members that are loving rather than making things difficult.

And here, let me just pause and address family members that are not suffering from OCD. Please, parents and siblings, please, cousins and relatives, educate yourself, educate yourself. OCD is something that is beyond the control of those who are having it. Please have some mercy and sympathy, have some love and compassion. Don't make things worse. Don't mock your brother or sister. Don't put your son or daughter in more trouble, a'udhu billah. Educate yourself. If you don't know, ask. If you don't know, find help from psychiatrists, from therapists.

Because a lot of times, and I'm sorry to be blunt here, your attitude is making that OCD a hundred times worse than it needs to be: your callousness, or your hard-heartedness, or your lack of understanding. Because maybe it's not callous in some cases, but it's a lack of understanding. They don't understand, and they're like, "Why are you spending so much time in the bathroom? Why are you washing your hands 50 times? Why are you doing wudu?" And they get irritated, and they don't understand that this OCD is something that needs to be treated in a different manner. It needs to be treated with love and compassion.

And also, by the way, sometimes it needs a type of medication as well. And again, you need to go to psychiatrists. It's not my area to tell you the specifics of this, but definitely go to a trained therapist. For some people, for some people, certain types of medications keep the OCD in check. So you need to ask and find out what is possible.

Also, another piece of advice that is given is to set achievable goals, very small, incremental, achievable goals. For a simple example, suppose that on average you're spending half an hour in the bathroom doing wudu over and over and over again, and you're washing, let's say, 10 times every limb. Make it your goal: "I'm never going to wash 10 times. I'm going to bring it down to, let's say, five times, if it ever happens again." Five times. Don't think you're going to go from 10 to 1 overnight; it might not happen. Or maybe from 10 to 8 even. Set your goal: "I'm never going to go more than this." Then when you get to that goal, thank Allah subhanahu wa ta'ala, and then try to minimize even more.

So work in increments. Work towards a goal that is reasonable for you, that's possible for you to do. Once you get it, alhamdulillah, it's an achievement. You've unlocked an achievement. From there, you reward yourself: you do something that is halal, permissible, that makes you happy, you thank Allah subhanahu wa ta'ala, and then you set the next goal, and then the next goal, and then the next goal.

And again, you start maybe one act at a time. Suppose you have this OCD complex in multiple areas; maybe it's not possible to simultaneously do all of them. So concentrate on one, for example, wudu. Concentrate on the wudu, and say, "InshaAllah, my goal is that day by day, week by week, I'm going to minimize the OCD when I'm doing wudu," by a set number, whatever number you put in your head. You calculate it out; you know best what's going to work for you. And then you have a coach, if you like, in your house, somebody that's supportive, and you report to them. They're going to work with you, and you set these realistic goals, and inshaAllah it will also help in this regard.

Also, many therapists advise keeping a journal as well, a private journal, a personal journal, where you share your thoughts, so that later on, when you read them, you realize, "Okay, you know what, next time I don't need to do that." So take a personal journal and express how you feel. And these days, of course, there are so many ways; you can even write it up and lock the file, put a password on it, so only you can read your personal thoughts. Because that also helps bounce your ideas off of yourself, so that, inshaAllah ta'ala, you can minimize this complex of continually doing the same act over and over again. So that's another thing that can be done.

Also, may I advise one other thing, and that is to listen to lots of Qur'an, to listen to Qur'an. I have also dealt with cases of this nature where reading the Qur'an and listening to the Qur'an actually helped the OCD. Therefore, try your best to have the Qur'an playing in the background, and maybe even put on earphones when you are doing wudu, for example. In this case, inshaAllah, it's permissible, because it's going to be in the earphones. You put your earphones on and you listen to some recitation of the Qur'an. I've had cases where, when they listen to the Qur'an, the OCD goes down a lot, which actually indicates that in that particular case the OCD was coming not even from them; it was coming from shaytan. So they have nothing to do with that. So all of these are some of the techniques that you can use.

And most importantly, don't lose hope. Don't feel anything negative or bad. You are not a bad person for having OCD, a'udhu billah. You're normal in your own way, and I'm normal in my own way. What is normal for you might not be normal for me; what is normal for me might not be normal for you. Allah created all of us in different ways. You have certain things you're struggling with; I have certain things I'm struggling with. And perhaps, in conquering your struggles, you have the opportunity to rise much higher than me and anybody else. So Allah has given you a task that He hasn't given me, and perhaps in conquering that task you are going to rise to higher heights than I can possibly go to. So don't view it as an impediment; view it as a challenge that Allah has also given you the tools to conquer.

Why? Because Allah says in the Qur'an, "Allah does not burden a soul with more than it can possibly carry." So any burden you have, and OCD is a type of burden, any burden that you have, Allah is telling us in the Qur'an that He knows you have the strength to conquer it. He knows you're able to overcome it. If He did not know this, if it was not true, you would not be in the situation. In other words, the fact that you are in this situation indicates Allah knows you can conquer the situation. Allah knows you have it in you to be able to rise up to the challenge and to be able to overcome this OCD.

So again, remember, dear brother and sister, that you don't feel bad or guilty. You are not leaving the faith and coming back in. You are not constantly having to do wudu. No, this is all from shaytan, and it's not from you. Do what needs to be done the proper way, and then try your best to eliminate all other thoughts. Definitely you do not have to act upon those thoughts, even if they come. Like I said, the goal is not necessarily elimination. If you're able to, that's great; try your best to eliminate. But if you're not able to eliminate, go ahead and accept the thought, but then conquer the action. Conquer the action, and say, "I'm not going to act upon this."

And realize, as I said, that **what is certain is not going to be gotten rid of by that which is doubtful.** Turn to Allah, make du'a to Allah subhanahu wa ta'ala, and inshaAllah ta'ala, bit by bit, slowly but surely, you will be able to overcome your OCD, to the point of your life becoming as normal as possible, alhamdulillah. And that is really the goal. May Allah 'azza wa jal make it easy for you.
